title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
formal:
Is there an integer constant \(C\ge1\) and a single uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite unweighted directed graph \(G\), returns an integer \(\widehat D\) satisfying
\[
\Pr\!\left[D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)\right]\ge 2/3
\]
and always halts in near-linear time? Here
\[
D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):u,v\in V(G),\ d_G(u,v)<\infty\}
\]
is the reachability diameter. The graph representation, machine and worst-case time bound are specified below. This retains the card's near-linear constant-factor specialization of the source's broader approximation-versus-time question; it does not ask to determine that entire tradeoff.
why: This asks whether a basic distance statistic of an arbitrary directed network can be estimated without computing distances from every vertex. It captures information that conventional directed diameter loses when directions are disconnected, and appears in assessing diameter reduction by reachability-preserving shortcut edges. A resolution would establish a general algorithmic principle or limitation for directed reachability and distance estimation.
definitions:
The input is a graph \(G=([n],E)\), where \(n\ge1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(E\subseteq[n]\times[n]\) is a set of directed edges. Loops are allowed, repeated edges are not, and every edge has length one. Write \(m=|E|\). A directed walk is a sequence \(v_0,\ldots,v_\ell\) with \((v_{j-1},v_j)\in E\) for \(1\le j\le\ell\), and has length \(\ell\). The distance \(d_G(u,v)\) is the minimum length of such a walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or \(\infty\) if no walk exists. Walks of length zero are permitted, so \(d_G(v,v)=0\), the displayed maximum is nonempty, and \(0\le D(G)\le n-1\). In particular, an edgeless graph has diameter zero. No connectivity, acyclicity or sparsity promise is imposed.

The input occupies \(O(n+m)\) read-only words: \(n,m\), an array of \(n+1\) offsets beginning with zero and ending with \(m\), and an array of \(m\) head labels. For each tail \(u\), the head labels between its two consecutive offsets list its outgoing neighbors without repetition, in arbitrary order. Correctness and cost bounds hold for every ordering of every valid list; there is no succinct encoding or separately supplied reachability information.

The algorithm is one finite program, independent of \(n,m,G\), with a fixed finite set of registers and random-access memory. For some fixed integer \(d\ge3\), a word has \(w=d\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits, represents an integer in \(\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), and can hold a memory address. Work cells are initially zero; only addresses in that range can be used. The program has the word width available but no advice, oracle, input-dependent program or precomputed table. In one step it may read or write one addressed word, copy a word, compare two words, branch, or perform one of addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer quotient, remainder, Boolean bitwise operations or a shift. Arithmetic results other than comparison are reduced modulo \(2^w\); quotient and remainder on divisor zero return zero; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Each instruction has fixed bounded arity. Reading one fresh independent fair random bit also costs one step. Input access, memory operations, random bits, preprocessing and writing the output all count.

Near-linear worst-case time means that there are fixed integers \(K\ge1\) and \(k\ge0\) such that, on every valid input and every sequence of random bits, the program halts with an integer output in \(\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) after at most
\[
K(n+m)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil^k
\]
steps. The probability in the target is over these independent random bits for each fixed input. Both underestimates outside the allowed interval and overestimates count as failure; no correctness requirement is imposed on the failure event beyond the output range. The constants \(C,d,K,k\) and program are chosen once before the universal quantification over inputs. There is no separate input approximation parameter and no restriction to combinatorial algorithms.

progress.text: The first arXiv version introduces the approximation/time landscape and leaves the best tradeoff for general unweighted directed graphs open. It distinguishes that question from reducing general graphs to acyclic ones.

The ESA version states in Theorem 7 a randomized additive-\(k\) approximation and in Theorem 9 a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Allowing logarithmic factors, the additive guarantee has time \(\widetilde O(nm/k)\) with high probability. The deterministic bound in Theorem 8 has an additional multiplicative factor and is restricted to acyclic graphs.

Corollary 5 conditionally rules out better-than-two approximation in time \(O(n^{\omega-\varepsilon})\), where \(\omega\) is the infimum exponent of arithmetic matrix multiplication and \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed. Its separate combinatorial version rules out truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms. Theorem 6 gives a conditional better-than-\(3/2\) barrier on sparse instances. These results concern bounded approximation factors and do not settle existence of some absolute constant factor in near-linear time.

context_blocks.text: Reachability diameter measures the longest shortest route that actually exists. Unreachable ordered pairs are omitted, so a one-way path on five vertices has reachability diameter four. This differs both from ordinary directed diameter, which becomes infinite if any ordered pair is unreachable, and from min-diameter, which uses the smaller of the two directional distances.

The source studies general directed graphs and separately asks whether the reachability-diameter problem can be reduced to directed acyclic graphs. Its hardness instances can already be acyclic, but this does not make an algorithm for acyclic inputs a solution for arbitrary inputs. Strong connectivity makes reachability diameter coincide with ordinary directed diameter and removes an essential part of the general question.

The card retains the specialization recorded in September 2026: a constant approximation in time \(\widetilde O(n+m)\), where the tilde permits a fixed power of \(\log n\). Open Problem 1 asks more broadly for the best approximation/time tradeoff. The explicit word operations, finite program, \(2/3\) success convention, integer output and worst-case clock make the inherited algorithmic model precise; the source does not itself spell out this complete RAM instruction set.

Theorem 7 gives additive approximation, and Theorem 9 gives a randomized near-linear-time \(n^{1/2+o(1)}\)-approximation. Neither supplies a constant multiplicative factor on every input. Additive error can dominate the diameter on small-diameter graphs, even when it is useful on graphs with long routes. The source also gives conditional barriers for sufficiently small approximation factors; those barriers do not rule out all constant factors.

answer_criterion: An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive answer must specify the finite uniform algorithm and constants \(C,d,K,k\), prove the stated time bound for every valid input and every random-bit sequence, and prove the approximation event has probability at least \(2/3\) for each such input. A negative answer must rule out every such choice of constants and program: for each candidate, either the required worst-case resource bound fails or some valid graph and encoding has approximation success probability less than \(2/3\). A conditional lower bound alone does not establish this unconditional negation. An algorithm only for acyclic, strongly connected, bounded-width or bounded-treewidth graphs does not establish the universal claim.

sentences: Reachability diameter is the largest finite shortest-path distance in an unweighted directed graph.
Ignoring unreachable pairs makes this statistic informative even when directions are disconnected.
The question asks for one randomized algorithm that gives a constant-factor estimate on every graph in near-linear worst-case time.
Known additive and polynomial-factor approximations, special graph classes and conditional small-factor barriers leave this target unresolved in the cited source.
A complete Lean proof must establish the universal algorithmic guarantee or rule it out in the stated model.

Root individually checked Theorems 7–9, Corollary 5, Theorem 6, and both open problems in the actual ESA text. The near-linear constant-factor yes/no question was already an explicit editorial specialization on this card, not the entire source tradeoff. Maintained that scope rather than silently changing to DAGs or the entire numerical tradeoff. The integer constant is without loss for the existence question by rounding a real constant upward. Integer-valued diameter supports an integral estimate convention; successful rational estimates can be rounded upward, preserving both bounds. Adding n to the usual tilde-m notation handles isolated vertices and explicit input representation.

Independent source audit by the parallel review agent confirmed the publisher date 25 August 2026 and checked actual arXiv v1 submitted 6 June 2026, with no later listed revision by 16 September. The conference PDF has 24 pages; the arXiv full version has 20. Table 1 is labelled for DAGs but Theorem 7 and Theorem 9 algorithms accept general directed graphs. Theorem 8 alone requires a DAG. The public card does not infer a general-to-DAG reduction from the table.

Runtime/probability caution from actual algorithm text: Theorem 7 states O(nm/k) and high probability, but Algorithm 3 on ESA page 21 samples O-tilde(n/k), whereas its proof mentions only 2n/k BFS runs. The latter constant sampling gives constant success for hitting a specified first k vertices. Public progress therefore uses the safe logarithm-suppressed bound at high probability and does not propagate a log-free high-probability assertion.

Theorem 9 does not explicitly say worst-case or expected time. Its argument on ESA page 22 invokes the shortcut construction of Jambulapati, Liu and Sidford. The independently read actual arXiv1905.08841v4 Lemma 4.3, PDF page 13/printed page 12, gives its near-linear runtime with probability at least 1-2n^{-10}. Public progress says randomized near-linear without attributing an always-worst-case clock to the literal published algorithm. A clocked Monte Carlo normalization can absorb rare slow executions into error, but that normalization is an editorial model choice, not a quoted theorem. The exact finite word-RAM convention makes the already-selected target reviewable.

Bounded later primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 included the paper title, reachability diameter, constant approximation, general directed graphs and shortcut sets, plus author publication lists. The ESA final version is itself only weeks old. The 2026 Structural parameterizations of Geodetic Set on directed (acyclic) graphs paper (arXiv2606.26414) concerns a different optimization task even when its instances have small reachability diameter. New parallel reachability and shortcut bounds do not by themselves approximate the original graph’s maximum finite distance. No matching resolution was located; this was not an exhaustive bibliography or verification of all proofs.
